title: Execution
summary: Execution is the tactic that covers adversary attempts to run their own code or abuse legitimate command interpreters on a victim system, and it is the bridge between having access and actually doing something with it. Concrete behaviours include launching PowerShell, cmd.exe, Windows Script Host, bash or other interpreters, using scheduled tasks and service creation to trigger payloads, exploiting client applications so that a document or archive executes code, and abusing built-in administration utilities that are already trusted and signed. Defenders see this tactic in process creation telemetry, command line logging, script block logging, module and image load events, application whitelisting or WDAC events, and, depending on maturity, EDR behavioural detections rather than simple indicator matches. The central problem is that execution telemetry is enormously high volume and heavily polluted by legitimate administrative activity. Management tooling, software deployment, monitoring agents, and helpdesk automation all spawn the same interpreters and utilities that attackers prefer, often with long encoded parameters. Detection in isolation therefore fails: a single encoded PowerShell command is weak evidence, whereas the same command spawning from an Office process, on a server that never runs interactive scripts, minutes after a new service was created, is a defensible finding. Effective work on this tactic means establishing a clean baseline of what runs where, enriching process events with parent-child lineage and signer information, and then hunting deviations from that baseline rather than chasing individual suspicious commands.
objectives: Describe the range of execution behaviours, from interpreter abuse and script hosts to scheduled task and service-based triggering.
Interpret process lineage and signer information to separate normal administrative execution from adversary execution.
Explain what Windows and Linux logging must be enabled before execution telemetry is usable at all, and what is lost when it is not.
Build detection logic that uses parent-child relationships and host role baselines instead of unreliable single-command signatures.
Recognise living-off-the-land execution patterns and describe why they defeat naive blocklists.
Trace an execution alert through to the persistence or command-and-control behaviour that follows it.
